# The framing effect in medical decision-making: a review of the literature

Jingjing Gong<sup>a,1</sup>, Yan Zhang<sup>b,1</sup>, Zheng Yang<sup>c</sup>, Yonghua Huang<sup>a</sup>, Jun Feng<sup>a</sup> and Weiwei Zhang<sup>a</sup>\*

<sup>a</sup>Department of Neurology, General Hospital of Beijing Command, Beijing, China; <sup>b</sup>Air force aviation medicine research Institute, Beijing, China; <sup>c</sup>Beijing Institute of Basic Medical Science, Beijing, China

(Received 7 July 2012; final version received 10 January 2013)

The framing effect, identified by Tversky and Kahneman, is one of the most striking cognitive biases, in which people react differently to a particular choice depending whether it is presented as a loss or as a gain. Numerous studies have subsequently demonstrated the robustness of the framing effect in a variety of contexts, especially in medical decision-making. Compared to daily decisions, medical decisions are of low frequency but of paramount importance. The framing effect is a well-documented bias in a variety of studies, but research is inconsistent regarding whether and how variables influence framing effects in medical decision-making. To clarify the discrepancy in the previous literature, published literature in the English language concerning the framing effect was retrieved using electronic and bibliographic searches. Two reviewers examined each article for inclusion and evaluated the articles' methodological quality. The framing effect in medical decision-making was reviewed in these papers. No studies identified an influence of framing information upon compliance with health recommendations, and different studies demonstrate different orientations of the framing effect. Because so many variables influence the presence or absence of the framing effect, the unexplained heterogeneity between studies suggests the possibility of a framing effect under specific conditions. Further research is needed to determine why the framing effect is induced and how it can be precluded.

Keywords: Framing effect; Medical decision-making; Treatment option; Detection behaviour; Prevention behaviour

## 1. Introduction

Decision-making is a process by which decision-makers judge, evaluate and make choices about behaviours or goals. Tversky and Kahneman (1981) first experimentally confirmed the concept of the “framing effect”: when making a decision, people may become biased towards one option due to the framing of the information. People are risk averse when information is presented positively, but they are risk seeking when equivalent information is presented negatively. For example, in Tversky and Kahneman’s (1981) landmark study on the framing effect, participants were presented with a classic framing effect problem, called the “Asian Disease” design. The scenarios are presented below.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">\*Corresponding author. Email: neuropsych@126.com</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>1</sup>The two authors contribute equally to this work.</span></small>

Imagine that the USA is preparing for the outbreak of an unusual Asian disease, which is expected to kill 600 people. Two alternative programmes to combat the disease have been proposed. Assume that the exact scientific estimation of the consequences of the programmes is as follows:

• Positive frame (Lives Saved Frame):

If Programme A is adopted, 200 people will be saved.

If Programme B is adopted, there is a one-third probability that 600 people will be saved and a two-thirds probability that no people will be saved.

Which of the two programmes would you favour?

• Negative frame (Lives Lost Frame):

If Programme C is adopted, 400 people will die.

If Programme D is adopted, there is a one-third probability that no one will die and a two-thirds probability that 600 people will die.

Which of the two programmes would you favour?

Obviously, both A and C are the same risk-averse options, whereas B and D are the identical risk-seeking options. However, participants were more likely to choose the risk-averse option (Programme A) when confronted with the positive frame and to choose the risk-seeking option (Programme D) when confronted with the negative frame. People influenced by different semantic descriptions of the same issue have different risk preferences (Kühberger, 1998). Since then, the framing effect has been a well-documented bias in a variety of studies (Kühberger, Schulte-Mecklenbeck, & Perner, 1999; Pinon and Gambara, 2005).

As a well-known behavioural economic theory that describes decisions between alternatives that involve risk where the probabilities of outcomes are known, prospect theory indicates that people make decisions according to the potential value of losses and gains rather than the final consequence. This theory is proposed to explain the framing effect, or to explain why goal outcomes may be affected by positively or negatively framed information that contains similar messages. In the medical field, many risky decisions must be made by doctors and patients in clinical practice. The framing effect is one of the most valuable approaches to investigating decisional biases and influencing factors in medical decision-making, and many studies have reported the framing effect in medical scenarios (McNeil, Pauker, Sox, & Tversky, 1982; Rothman et al., 1999; Armstrong et al., 2002). We aimed to review the literature on the framing effect in medical decision-making and to compare the influence of the framing effect on different types of medical decisions.

## 2. Method

## 2.1. Eligibility criteria

We included studies that enrolled individuals with indirect or direct experience of conditions for which medical choices were made. We specifically included studies that examined the effect of framing upon participants:

• studies that examined how a participant’s preference was changed in the context of consideration of different types and presentations of treatment;

• studies that examined decision-making when participants were presented with different health-related behaviours and addictive behaviours.

We excluded studies that were not available in English.

## 2.2. Search strategy

Published literature in the English language concerning the framing effect was retrieved using electronic and bibliographic searches. We searched Medline, ScienceDirect and ProQuest Digital Dissertation (2005–2012), and we reviewed the reference lists of all eligible studies. We retrieved the full texts of articles judged potentially eligible by at least one reviewer. Two reviewers independently examined each article for inclusion and evaluated the methodological quality.

## 3. Result

## 3.1. Framework, types of treatment and data format influence medical treatment options

In 1982, McNeil and colleagues first investigated the influence of framing on medical decision-making. They found the presence of a framing effect when participants were asked to select between hypothetical treatments (radiation or surgery) for lung cancer. Information was framed in terms of either survival or mortality rates, and the data format was modulated, including a cumulative probability format and an overall life expectancy format (see Table 1). The participants preferred to choose surgery when the information was presented in terms of survival, and they chose radiation when information was framed in terms of mortality, which occurred in both data formats. Interestingly, compared with the classical framing effect, the medical framework yields a reversed pattern during the decision process: the risk-seeking option is preferred in the positive frame and the risk-averse choice is favoured in the negative frame (McNeil et al., 1982). An interval probability format was added to the scenarios by Tengs (1987), who found the same pattern of responses as McNeil et al. (1982).

Numerous studies have shown that the framing effect was induced when medical treatment options were presented in terms of the probability of survival or mortality (Armstrong et al., 2002). If invasive treatments (e.g. surgery) were involved in medical scenarios, these treatments were more preferred in a positive frame than a negative frame. A similar study was performed by Almashat et al. (2008), who found that younger adults presented with a cumulative probability format preferred surgery in the survival scenario and radiation in the mortality scenario. However, this framing effect was absent in the interval probability format or the overall life expectancy format, demonstrating that in medical decision-making, the framework and types of outcome information exert effects on treatment choices.

Table 1. Examples of different data formats for the mortality of surgery for lung cancer.

| Data format | Examples (Stoner, 2007) |
| --- | --- |
| Cumulative probability | Of 100 patients having surgery, 10 die during the treatment, 32 die by one year and 66 die by 5years |
| Overall life expectancy | Of 100 patients having surgery, 10% of the patients die during treatment. The patients who survive surgery have an average life expectancy of 6.8years |
| Interval probability | Of 100 patients having surgery, 10 patients die by the end of treatment, 22 patients die in the interval between treatment and one year, 34 patients die in the interval between one and five years and 34 patients die sometime after five years |

However, not all medical frameworks yield a reversed pattern during the decision process. Perneger and Agoritsas (2011) studied framing bias in doctors and patients by rating whether a new drug was more effective than an old drug. Four different framing formats were presented: absolute survival (new drug 96% vs. old drug 94%), absolute mortality (4% vs. 6%), relative mortality reduction (reduction by one-third) or all three (fully informed condition). The new drug was reported to cause more side effects. Therefore, the new drug would be considered a risk-seeking option. The authors found that the proportion of doctors who rated the new drug more effective varied by the risk presentation format (absolute survival 51.8%, absolute mortality 68.3%, relative mortality reduction 93.8% and fully informed condition 69.8%, $p   <   0 . 0 0 1 )$ , indicating that the risk-seeking option (the new drug) was preferred in the negative frame (high rating in absolute mortality and relative mortality reduction).

## 3.2. Prevention behaviours are influenced by framework and other factors

If the gains of some behavioural performances are provided to individuals, preventive behaviours may be promoted (Detweiler et al., 1999; Mann et al., 2004). This suggestion was supported by a study of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine (Bigman, Cappella, & Hornik, 2010). This study found that respondents exposed to positive framing (70% effective) rated the HPV vaccine more effective and were more supportive of the vaccine mandate policy than were those exposed to the negative frame (30% ineffective) or the control frame. By contrast, the advantages of negatively framed information to elicit willingness to engage in preventive behaviours have been observed in other studies (O’Connor, Ferguson, & $\mathrm { O ^ { \prime } C o n n o r } ,$ 2005). A study investigated the effect of the framing and focus of health messages on intentions to perform skin protection behaviours and the perceived threat of skin cancer. The study found that intentions to perform preventive behaviours were greater for loss-framed messages (Thomas et al., 2011).

Nevertheless, some studies have reported no differences in the intention to engage in preventive behaviours across different frames (Rivers et al., 2005). With regard to the limited support for the use of framing to increase the persuasiveness of health messages in previous studies, Gallagher and Updegraff (2012) distinguished the outcomes used to assess the persuasive impact of framed messages in their meta-analysis. Their findings showed that gain-framed messages were more likely than loss-framed messages to encourage prevention behaviours $(r=0.083,\ p=0.002)$ , particularly for skin cancer prevention, smoking cessation and physical activity, supporting the tendency for positive framing to be more persuasive in promoting prevention behaviours than negative framing.

Framing effects on preventive behaviours are also moderated by other external or internal factors. A study of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine examined whether the effectiveness of loss-framed information was enhanced by the presence of a peripheral threat cue, the colour red. The study found that vaccination intentions were higher among participants exposed to a loss-framed message than to a gain-framed message, but only when the participants were primed with red (not grey, the control colour) (Gerend & Sias, 2009). Chien (2011) identified an interaction between framing biases and colour combinations by examining the effects of message framing (gain vs. loss) and colour combinations (red background with white characters vs. white background with black characters) on participants' perceptions of materials promoting the H1N1 flu vaccine and their willingness to receive the vaccine after reading the materials. The results showed that the participants rated vaccine information presented through loss-framed messages as more interesting. Moreover, loss-framed messages presented on a white background with black characters significantly increased the willingness of the participants to receive the vaccine.

## 3.3. Effect of framing upon detection behaviours is modulated by different variables

Previous research has studied the effect of positive or negative frameworks on the promotion of health-related behaviour. Meyerowitz and Chaiken (1987) found that there were no differences between groups in their willingness to perform early detection behaviour until 4 months later. After 4 months, female college students who received negative framing reported a preference to engage in early detection behaviours. Since then, a growing body of research has examined the relations between the framing effect and the promotion of detection behaviours, including the use of mammograms (Banks, Salovey, Greener, & Rothman, 1995) and screening for prostate cancer (Cherubini, Rumiati, Rossi, Nigro, & Calabro, 2005).

Previous research has demonstrated that loss-framed messages are more effective than gain-framed messages in motivating detection behaviours (Rothman et al., 1999). However, similar to observations of the effect of framed information on preventive behaviours, there is no consistency in the domain of detection behaviours. Some studies have indicated that positively framed messages seem to be more persuasive in encouraging participants to perform detection behaviours than negatively framed messages (Apanovitch et al., 2003). Furthermore, some studies have investigated different detection behaviours and failed to find differences across frames (Arora, 2000; Williams, Clarke, & Borland, 2001). A recent meta-analysis (Gallagher and Updegraff, 2012) failed to show a significant effect of framing when persuasion was assessed by attitudes/intentions or among studies encouraging detection.

Framing effects on detection behaviours are also mediated by certain variables. The first variable is perceived susceptibility to the disease. It was reported in a study that the effect of message framing on screening was only modulated by perceived susceptibility to breast cancer. Women with average and higher levels of perceived susceptibility to breast cancer were significantly more likely to report screening after viewing negatively framed information compared to positively framed information. However, there were no effects of framing on reported screening for women with lower levels of perceived susceptibility, indicating a key role for perceived susceptibility in shaping responses to framed messages that promote cancer screening (Gallagher, Updegraff, Rothman, & Sims, 2011).

The second variable is culture. A study by Han and Jo (2012) examined how culture influenced the persuasive effects of health campaigns promoting early screening for cancers occurring in women. Two message dimensions were included: individualistic vs. collectivistic appeal and gain vs. loss framing (see Table 2). The authors found that message framing alone did not significantly influence the effectiveness of public campaigns for women’s cancer prevention, which was similar across three countries (the USA, South Korea and Japan). Gain-framed messages were more likely to be persuasive when combined with collectivistic appeal, whereas loss-framed messages tended to be more effective when combined with an individualistic appeal in both the USA and South Korea, but this result was not found for Japan.

Table 2. Examples of message dimensions (individualistic vs. collectivistic appeal and gain vs. loss frame) for participants in the USA.

| Appeal | Frame | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individualistic | Gain | If little concern can protect your health and happiness |
| Collectivistic | Gain | If little concern can protect your family's happiness |
| Individualistic | Loss | If little neglect can rob your health and happiness |
| Collectivistic | Loss | If little neglect can rob your family's health and happiness |

Finally, some researchers have assessed the influence of gain- and loss-framed messages and visual aids upon affective reactions, risk perceptions, attitudes, behavioural intentions and reported behaviours related to the prevention and detection of STDs. The results indicated that gain-framed messages induced greater adherence to preventive behaviours, whereas loss-framed messages were more effective in promoting illnessdetecting behaviours (Garcia-Retamero & Cokely, 2011).

## 3.4. Addictive behaviours are affected by message framing and level of dependency

Researchers are increasingly focusing on addictive behaviours, such as nicotine and alcohol. For example, Marjolein Moorman and Putte (2008) explored the combined effect of message framing, intention to quit smoking and nicotine dependence on the persuasiveness of smoking cessation messages (see Table 3). It was suggested that smokers' intentions to quit smoking and their level of nicotine dependence affected the persuasiveness of positive and negative message frames. Specifically, a positive message frame should be chosen to help with quitting smoking when the level of nicotine dependence or quitting intention is low. By contrast, a negative frame is preferable when nicotine dependence and quitting intention are both high (Marjolein Moorman &

Putte, 2008). Nicotine dependence was studied as a moderator of a quitline-based message framing intervention by Fucito et al. (2011), who found that gain-framed messages resulted in less variable smoking outcomes than standard-care messages. These findings lend support to prior research demonstrating nicotine dependence heterogeneity in response to message framing interventions.

## 4. Discussion

Health is closely related to behaviours that prevent or detect health problems. Some studies have demonstrated that people are more easily persuaded of the importance of prevention or detection behaviours in positively framed conditions than in negatively framed conditions (Detweiler et al., 1999). However, other researchers have drawn opposite conclusions (Bank et al., 1995). Unfortunately, there is no consensus in previous studies about the influence of the framing effect on health behaviours. Different functions of goal-related health behaviours may account for the inconsistency of a persuasive frame (Rothman and Salovey, 1997). For example, preventive behaviours are performed to protect participants from injuries or uncomfortable outcomes, whereas detection behaviours are used to determine whether people suffer from certain diseases, which indicates different probabilities for an aversive consequence.

Based on the literature mentioned above, we identified the influence of the framing effect on medical treatment. Generally speaking, invasive treatments are more preferred in a positive frame than in a negative frame, whereas new drugs were more favoured in a negative frame than in a positive frame. Notably, the data format may affect the presence and absence of the framing effect. It is accepted that the intention to engage in preventive behaviours is significantly increased by positive framing. In addition, the message effects of framing on preventive behaviours are moderated by other variables, such as the presence of a peripheral threat cue, perceived effectiveness in preventing a risk and susceptibility to the risk. It has been suggested that health detection behaviours are promoted by the description of losses even without performing such detection behaviours.

In the original study of the framing effect, participants were asked to decide between a risky choice and a risk-averse preference in a scenario concerning a hypothetical disease (Asian diseases). This design with fictitious scenarios has been imitated by subsequent researchers, which is indicative of the long distance from these studies findings to their application in daily life. Unfortunately, excessive numbers of young adults (e.g. college students or undergraduate participants) are recruited in studies of the framing effect on healthcare decision-making (Almashat et al., 2008), especially for medical treatment (for example, radiation or surgery). Few studies have investigated the framing effect among older adults, who are the majority of medical decision-makers. For example, when Meyerowitz and Chaiken (1987) investigated the influence of the framing effect on health-related behaviours (breast self-examination as an approach to early detection of breast cancer), they chose female college students as participants. McElroy and Seta (2003) found that if the scenario was highly related to the participants, the framing effect diminished or disappeared. Many unreliable and questionable conclusions have been produced by studies in which most of the medical scenarios are not related to the healthy younger participants. Many researchers have begun to acknowledge such problems, as Peters et al. (2010) admitted: “The generalizability of the findings is limited due to the use of non-patients, presented a hypothetical scenario. Given the design, one cannot know whether observed differences would translate into clinically significant differences in patient behaviors”. Therefore, the ultimate option is that people “… need to know under what conditions, for which behaviors, and for who are gain-framed or loss-framed messages most persuasive” (Schneider et al., 2001).

As mentioned above, the effects of framing on health-related behaviours are modulated by many variables, such as culture, data format, peripheral threat cues and visual aids. These variables must be explored simultaneously in future studies. Moreover, there may be many variables that remain undefined, which may partly account for the inconsistency in the literature. Therefore, further studies are required to identify new factors that influence the framing effect on medical decision-making. Akl et al. (2011) noted that attributes and goal framing have little if any consistent effect on health consumers' behaviour. That is, not all studies find an influence of framing information on compliance with health recommendations, and different studies demonstrate different orientations of the framing effect. The unexplained heterogeneity between studies suggests the possibility of a framing effect under specific conditions, which implies that such conditions must be investigated further in future research.
